cards.ask: State it — and the reason behind it.
a: In HX addition to an alkene, H goes to the carbon that already has more H, and X to the more substituted carbon.
Protonation goes through the more stable (more substituted) carbocation; X ends up where the positive charge was.

cards.ask: Which alkene does an ordinary elimination favor?
a: The more substituted, more stable alkene is the major product.
A bulky base (e.g. t-BuO⁻) or a bulky leaving group (Hofmann elimination) gives the less substituted alkene.

cards.ask: What makes a ring aromatic?
a: Cyclic, planar, a p orbital on every ring atom (fully conjugated), and 4n + 2 π electrons: 2, 6, 10, 14…
Not aromatic. Cyclic, planar and conjugated with 4n π electrons is antiaromatic.

cards.ask: Reagents, mechanism, and the constraint?
a: An alkoxide (RO⁻, often from ROH + NaH) displaces a halide: RO⁻ + R′X → R–O–R′.
The halide must be methyl or primary; on a secondary or tertiary halide the alkoxide acts as a base and E2 wins.

cards.ask: Reagents, and how is the yield pushed up?
a: Carboxylic acid + alcohol, with an acid catalyst (H⁺) → ester + water.
It is an equilibrium: use the alcohol in excess or remove the water as it forms.

cards.ask: What does it make, and why does it stop cleanly?
a: Phthalimide (N–H pK<sub>a</sub> about 8.3) is deprotonated by KOH, alkylated once by RX in an SN2, then the amine is released (hydrazine or hydrolysis).
The alkylated nitrogen has no N–H left, so it cannot be alkylated a second time.

cards.ask: Substrate, reagents, product?
a: Primary amide + Br2, NaOH → primary amine with one fewer carbon.
The alkyl group migrates from the carbonyl carbon to N, giving an isocyanate that hydrolyzes and loses that carbon as CO<sub>2</sub>.

cards.ask: How is it related to the Hofmann rearrangement?
a: An acyl azide (acid chloride + NaN<sub>3</sub>) is heated → isocyanate → primary amine.
Same isocyanate, same lost carbon: the amine has one carbon fewer than the acid.

cards.ask: Reagents, and what makes it controllable?
a: Ketone or aldehyde + an amine (or NH<sub>3</sub>), then NaBH<sub>3</sub>CN → amine.
The imine (or iminium) forms first and is reduced in the same pot.
You choose 1°, 2° or 3° by the amine you start with, and it does not over-alkylate the way direct alkylation does.

cards.ask: Steps, and which alkene?
a: Exhaustive methylation with excess CH<sub>3</sub>I → quaternary ammonium salt; Ag<sub>2</sub>O/H<sub>2</sub>O swaps in hydroxide; heat → E2.
The less substituted (Hofmann) alkene: the bulky NR3 leaving group makes the base take the least hindered β-H.

cards.ask: Reagents, and what makes it better than an elimination?
a: Ph3P + a methyl or primary alkyl halide (SN2) → phosphonium salt; strong base (n-BuLi or NaH) → ylide; ylide + aldehyde or ketone → alkene + Ph3P=O.
The C=C forms exactly where the C=O was — no Zaitsev mixture, no rearrangement.

cards.ask: What reacts with what, and what is required of the diene?
a: A conjugated diene (4 π e⁻) + a dienophile (2 π e⁻) → a cyclohexene, in one concerted [4+2] cycloaddition; two new C–C σ bonds form at once.
Must be able to reach the s-cis conformation.
Stereospecific: groups cis on the dienophile stay cis in the ring.

cards.ask: The two stages, and what decides where it stops?
a: An enolate adds to a second carbonyl → β-hydroxy aldehyde or ketone.
Dehydration of that product → α,β-unsaturated carbonyl (enone) + water.
Mild and short stops at the addition product; heat drives the condensation.

cards.ask: Partners, product, and why a full equivalent of base?
a: Ester enolate + a second ester (acyl substitution) → β-keto ester + alkoxide.
Needs a full equivalent (the alkoxide matching the ester): the β-keto ester is deprotonated (α-H pK<sub>a</sub> about 11), and that step pulls the equilibrium over. Acid workup restores it.

cards.ask: What is it?
a: An intramolecular Claisen: a diester closes to a cyclic β-keto ester.
Five- and six-membered rings form well; a 1,6-diester (e.g. diethyl adipate) gives a five-membered ring.

cards.ask: Donor, acceptor, product?
a: A stabilized enolate or enamine (1,3-dicarbonyl, malonate, β-keto ester, nitroalkane).
Conjugate (1,4) addition at the β carbon → a 1,5-dicarbonyl.

cards.ask: Which two reactions, and what does it build?
a: Michael addition (usually to methyl vinyl ketone), then an intramolecular aldol condensation.
A new six-membered ring containing an α,β-unsaturated ketone (a cyclohexenone).

cards.ask: Steps and product?
a: Diethyl malonate + NaOEt → enolate; alkylate with RX (SN2); hydrolyze (H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>) and heat to decarboxylate.

cards.ask: Steps and product?
a: Ethyl acetoacetate + NaOEt → enolate; alkylate with RX (SN2); hydrolyze and heat to decarboxylate.

cards.ask: Reagents, product, and why the phosphorus?
a: Carboxylic acid + Br<sub>2</sub> with catalytic PBr<sub>3</sub> (or red P) → α-bromo carboxylic acid.
An acid barely enolizes; PBr<sub>3</sub> converts it to the acyl bromide, which does, and that enol is what brominates.

cards.ask: Substrate, reagents, products?
a: The carboxylate RCOO⁻ (one carbon shorter) + CHX<sub>3</sub> (e.g. iodoform, CHI<sub>3</sub>).
In base each halogen makes the next α-H more acidic, so the CH<sub>3</sub> is halogenated three times.

cards.ask: Steps, and why does it stop after one alkylation?
a: Ketone + a secondary amine (mild acid) → enamine; alkylate or acylate the α carbon; hydrolyze → α-substituted ketone.
Alkylation turns the enamine into an iminium salt, which has no nucleophilic carbon left.

cards.ask: Reagent, product, and which group migrates?
a: Ketone + a peroxyacid (e.g. mCPBA) → ester; a cyclic ketone → lactone.
H > 3° > 2° ≈ cyclohexyl ≈ benzyl ≈ aryl > 1° > methyl. The O is inserted on that group’s side.
The migrating group keeps its configuration.

cards.ask: Reagents and product?
a: Na or Li in liquid NH<sub>3</sub>, with an alcohol as the proton source.
A non-conjugated cyclohexa-1,4-diene — the ring is only partly reduced.

cards.ask: What do both do, and how do you choose?
a: Reduce the C=O of a ketone or aldehyde all the way to CH<sub>2</sub>. Not esters or amides.
Hydrazine, then KOH and heat — strongly basic. Use it when the molecule cannot survive acid.

cards.ask: Reagent, positive result, and what it tells you?
a: A silver mirror: the aldehyde is oxidized (to the carboxylate) and Ag<sup>+</sup> is reduced to Ag metal.
Aldehyde present; ordinary ketones do not react.

cards.ask: Where does it brominate, and why NBS rather than Br₂?
a: The benzylic (or allylic) C–H, by a radical chain.
It keeps the Br<sub>2</sub> concentration very low, so ionic addition of Br<sub>2</sub> to any C=C cannot compete.

cards.ask: Reagents and product?
a: Phenoxide + CO<sub>2</sub> (about 125 °C, pressure), then acid workup → salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid).
The phenoxide’s negative charge is delocalized onto the ortho and para carbons, so a ring carbon attacks the CO<sub>2</sub>.

cards.ask: What does a carbonyl compound need, and what is lost?
a: A hydrogen on the γ carbon.
Through a six-membered ring the γ-H moves to the carbonyl O and the α–β bond breaks.
A neutral alkene; the ion detected is an enol radical cation.

cards.ask: Reagents and product?
a: Aldehyde + NH<sub>3</sub> + HCN → α-amino nitrile (imine, then cyanide adds); hydrolyze the nitrile → α-amino acid.
Racemic: the new stereocenter forms at a planar imine.

cards.ask: Reagent, and what does it tell you?
a: Phenyl isothiocyanate, PhN=C=S, then mild acid.
Removes the N-terminal residue as a phenylthiohydantoin, which is identified — then repeats on the shortened peptide. It sequences from the N-terminus, one residue at a time.

cards.ask: What is it, and what does it give you?
a: TiCl<sub>4</sub> with a trialkylaluminum such as Al(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>3</sub>.
Stereoregular polymers — isotactic polypropylene — because every monomer adds the same way at the metal.
